title: Review: Electric field strength and field lines; Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium; Electric potential and potential energy; Charged particles in uniform electric fields
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics 2 (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: F05-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; F08-ap1#t2 term and clue written for the game; F03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; F08-ap1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: F03-1#N.11, F04-1#N.5b, F04-ap1#N.2a, F05-1#N.14, F08-1#N.5b, F08-ap1#N.5, F03-1#N.7b, F04-1#N.7b, F04-ap1#N.6, F05-1#N.15, F08-1#N.8, F08-ap1#N.6. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Weight
items.clue: Pull of gravity: about 10⁻²⁹ N on an electron, so negligible here.

items.label: Equipotential
items.clue: What joined conductors form: every part of the surface at the same V.

items.label: Electric field
items.clue: Region where a charge feels a force, present even with nothing placed in it.

items.label: Grounding
items.clue: Joining an object to the planet with a conductor, leaving it almost neutral.

questions.stem: The field lines of a long, straight charged wire spread out radially, in planes at right angles to the wire: they spread in two dimensions, not three. Point P is 2.0 cm from the wire and point Q is 6.0 cm from it, both far from the wire's ends. How does the electric field strength at P compare with that at Q?

options.text: E at P is 9 times E at Q, as the field strength falls with the square of the distance.
E at P is 3 times E at Q, as the same lines spread over 3 times the area at Q.
E is the same at P and Q, as every line that passes P also passes Q.
E at Q is 3 times E at P, as the larger cylinder at Q holds more lines.

questions.stem: An electron is released from rest at a location where the electric potential is 50 V. Moving under the electric force alone, it reaches a location where the electric potential is 250 V. How much kinetic energy has it gained? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

Three particles, each with charge +q, are fixed on a straight line at x = −d, x = 0 and x = +d. A student claims that the system's total electric potential energy is kq²/(2d), reasoning that the middle particle's interactions with the two outer particles cancel. Which evaluation of the claim is best supported?

options.text: Correct: the forces on the middle particle cancel, so its two pair energies cancel.
Incorrect: each particle has its own share of each pair, so U_E is 5kq²/d.
Incorrect: U_E is a scalar, so all three pair energies add, giving 5kq²/(2d).
Incorrect: each pair's U_E depends on 1/r², so U_E is 9kq²/(4d²).

questions.stem: A proton and an alpha particle are placed, one at a time, at the same point in a uniform electric field. The alpha particle has twice the charge of the proton and about four times its mass. Gravity is negligible. What is the ratio (acceleration of the alpha particle) / (acceleration of the proton)?
questions.explanation: Correct. Acceleration = charge × E ÷ mass, so the ratio is (2/4) = 1/2. The alpha particle accelerates half as much.

questions.stem: A metal sphere of radius 0.10 m, far from other charged objects, carries a charge of +4.0 × 10⁻⁸ C. Use k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the magnitude of the electric field at a point 0.20 m from the sphere's surface?
A metal sphere on an insulating stand has a charge of +5.0 nC. It is then connected to Earth by a metal wire, with no other charged objects nearby. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Positive charge flows off the sphere and down the wire into the Earth.
Charge flows until the sphere and the Earth hold equal amounts of charge.
No charge flows, as the neutral Earth exerts no electric force.
Electrons flow from Earth onto the sphere until it is almost neutral.

questions.stem: A particle with charge +q is fixed a distance 2d to the left of point P, and a particle with charge +3q is fixed a distance 3d to the right of P. Which expression gives the magnitude of the net electric field at P?

options.text: 2kq/(25d²)
kq/(4d²)
kq/(12d²)

questions.stem: System X consists of two protons, and system Y consists of a proton and an electron. In each system an external force moves the two particles farther apart. For which system or systems does the electric potential energy increase?

options.text: Only for system Y, the proton and electron
Only for system X, the pair of protons
For both systems, as the particles separate
For neither system, since U_E falls as r grows

questions.stem: A proton and an electron are each released from rest beside one plate of a pair of oppositely charged parallel plates in vacuum: the proton beside the positive plate and the electron beside the negative plate. Each moves under the electric force alone to the opposite plate. Which particle arrives with the greater speed, and why?

options.text: Neither: charges of equal magnitude give them equal final speeds.
The electron: both gain equal kinetic energy, and its mass is smaller.
The proton: the electron moves to higher potential, raising its U_E.
The electron: its larger acceleration gives it more kinetic energy.

questions.stem: In the worked example, the electron left the plates deflected sideways by a distance y. The potential difference across the plates is now doubled, and the electron enters at twice the speed. What is its sideways deflection at exit now?

options.text: y
2y

questions.explanation: y = ½at², with a ∝ |ΔV| (×2) and t = L/v (×½, so t² × ¼). The deflection is 2 × ¼ = ½ of y.

questions.stem: A solid lump of metal with a sharp point at one end carries excess charge and has settled. Which statement is correct?

options.text: E is zero inside the metal near the point; the excess charge is all on the outer surface.
E is strong inside the metal near the point, because the charge crowds toward the point.
E is zero everywhere inside the metal; the excess charge is spread evenly through it.
E is zero only at the centre of the lump; near the point inside, it is not zero.

questions.explanation: In equilibrium no free electron is pushed anywhere inside the metal, so E = 0 at every interior point, whatever the shape. Any excess charge inside would make a field there, so it all sits on the outer surface.

questions.stem: An isolated metal sphere of radius R is charged to a potential V₀, taking the potential to be zero far away. It is then connected by a long, thin wire to a distant, uncharged metal sphere of radius 3R. The wire carries a negligible charge. What is the potential of the first sphere once equilibrium is reached?
